about: The abbreviation vocabulary for nexus/consistency-no-abbreviated-identifier, read by the Go rule through go:embed and by the Swift engine directly. Each entry is one abbreviated word: `expansions` are the words it stands in for, the most common meaning first, and each form says where in a name the word is judged. A suffix or segment form matches the word capitalized, and suggests the expansion capitalized. A word with more than one common meaning lists every one, and its messages name them all and ask for whichever it means, never one guess; a word whose meanings are too many to list, or one of whose meanings has no full word to expand to, has no `expansions` and gives its `advice` instead. Only the Go engine fixes a name from this file, and only where a finding names one spelling, so a single expansion promises the rename is right wherever the word appears: a word with more than one expansion must never be fixed, since only its author knows which it means. Order is observable: within each form the rule reports the first entry that matches, so `ms` sits between `params` and `ref`, the early prefixes run `ctx` through `prev` in this order, and `vars` precedes `var`. Framework exemptions (`params` in route files, `ref` in React property positions, `config` in middleware, TanStack's `queryFn`) are policy rather than vocabulary and stay in the Go rule.

abbreviations.reason: A millisecond unit read as a camelCase word: a lowercase letter before it, and the end of the name or the next word after, so `maximumAgeMsHalf` counts while `SMS`, `LLMs` and `msgText` do not. The tree spells the unit `InMilliseconds`, more than two to one over `Ms` for the identical value.

abbreviations.advice: Use "argument", "commandArgument", or a more descriptive name.
abbreviations.reason: The whole word and the prefix give advice rather than one rename, because the right name depends on what the argument is.

abbreviations.advice: Use "arguments", "commandArguments", "commandLineArguments", or a more descriptive name.
abbreviations.reason: `arguments` is a reserved binding, so the whole word and the prefix give advice rather than the bare expansion.

abbreviations.advice: Pick a name that describes what is being accumulated, "total", "sum", "groupedItems", or whatever fits the reduce.
abbreviations.reason: A reduce accumulator has no single expansion: the right name is whatever it accumulates.

abbreviations.advice: Use "callback", "handler", "factory", or a more descriptive name.
abbreviations.reason: A function wants a role rather than an expansion: `function` names the kind, not the job.

suffix.advice: Use a more descriptive name, drop the "Fn" suffix or rename to a role like "Handler", "Callback", "Factory".

abbreviations.reason: It has four common meanings, so every message names them all. A census of the Go fix's renames found it meaning a result, MakeMap's reserve and result types, never a response.
An early prefix: judged before any suffix, so a name starting with it reports the prefix even when it also ends with an abbreviation.

A segment ends at the end of the name or the start of the next word, which is what keeps `Direction` from reading as `Dir`. It has two common meanings: a census of the Go fix's renames found it naming a ChanDir's direction as well as a directory, so every message names both.

abbreviations.advice: Use "Variables" for variables, or a name saying it means JavaScript's var keyword.
abbreviations.reason: Before `var`, so the longer word wins. It asks rather than offering `Variables` for the reason `var` does: a census of the Go fix's renames found `Var` and `Vars` in names meaning JavaScript's var keyword, which is no variable.

abbreviations.advice: Use "Variable" for a variable, or a name saying it means JavaScript's var keyword.
abbreviations.reason: A census of the Go fix's renames found names like `NoVar` meaning JavaScript's var keyword, which is no variable, and the keyword has no full word to expand to, so it asks rather than offering `Variable`. KeywordTerms.json lists the names in which `Var` is the keyword, `isVarDeclaration` among them, and those read clean.

The thirteen from `buf` to `sb` are Go's everyday abbreviations, added for every engine by @system_cohere's ruling on #ec8mvbg so the house keeps one vocabulary. Each is judged as the whole name, as a prefix followed by a capital, and as a segment, so only a whole camelCase word counts: `Buffer` and `Buffalo` never read as `Buf`.

Every form needs a word boundary after it, so `Posix` and `Post` never read as `Pos`. It has two common meanings: a census found `resultPos` beside `resultNeg`, where it means positive, so every message names both.

Every form needs a word boundary after it, so `Check` and `Change` never read as `Ch`. It has two common meanings: a census of the Go fix's renames found it naming a rune as well as a channel, so every message names both.

Go's habit reads `sb` as a strings.Builder, but a census found it naming a scroll region's bottom, and the letters fit more words than a list could hold, so every form asks for the name rather than guessing one.

This word and the ones after it, to `deref`, are the abbreviations go/ast, go/types and go/ir taught Go code, added for every engine by #r0fa8pa and #2xt6v5r after a census of every consumer, each with the forms the thirteen Go words carry: the whole name, a prefix followed by a capital, and a segment. Every form needs a word boundary after the abbreviation, so `Instruction`, `Successor`, `Program`, `Condition`, `Change`, `Expression`, `Function`, `Open`, `Operation`, `Select`, `Self`, `Type` and `Typical` never read as one. `instrs` is go/ir's list of a block's instructions, kept though the census found none on the Mac, and precedes `instr` as `vars` precedes `var`.
The census found it meaning an instruction in all 30 of its findings, the IR's and api's chat instructions alike.
go/ir's list of a block's successors, kept beside `succ` though the census found none on the Mac.
The census found it naming a block's successor in all 5 of its findings. `Success` and `Succeed` never read as it.
go/ir's list of a block's predecessors, which the census found in a static single assignment builder too.
The census found it naming a block's predecessor in all 5 of its findings. `Predicate` and `Predict` never read as it.
The census found it naming the IR's Program in all 22 of its findings. `Progress` never reads as it.
The census found it naming the IR's Allocation in all 4 of its findings, never the verb. `Allocate` and `Allocator` never read as it.
The census found it meaning an address in all 24 of its findings: a shipping address, an IP range's address, and the IR's addresses.
Before `cond`, so the longer word wins. The census found it naming the IR's branch conditions.
The census found it meaning a condition in all 22 of its findings: the IR's branch conditions and ESLint's no-cond-assign, whose Go names spell the rule.
go/ir's spelling for a channel, kept as #r0fa8pa names it though the census found none on the Mac. `Change` and `Channel` never read as it.
The census found it meaning an expression in all 62 of its findings: go/ast's in the IR, SQL's in api's Drizzle adapters, TypeScript's in a GraphQL document pass.

abbreviations.advice: Use a name for its role, as "callback", "handler" or "factory", or a more descriptive name ending in "Function".
abbreviations.reason: The census found it meaning a function in all 290 of its findings, Go's `XxxFunc` function types and ESLint's func-name-matching, no-func-assign, no-loop-func and no-new-func among them. The whole word gives advice rather than the bare expansion, since `function` is reserved in TypeScript, as `arguments` is for `args`, and a bare `func` is a keyword in Go and Swift.
The census found it naming a token.FileSet in all 9 of its findings.

It has two meanings, so every message names both: the census found it naming a method's receiver in most of its 25 findings, and a receive in the rest, a select case's `<-ch` and the IR's Receive instruction.

It has three meanings, so every message names them all: the census found an operation (api's batch operations, ahra's diff operations, a no-op), an operator (a finance rule's match operator, the IR's token) and an operand (the IR's `for _, op := range ops`). `BinOp` and `UnOp` read as `Op` and get the same message. `ops` is no entry: the census found it naming the Ops portal, a product area and its `/ops` route in four apps, in most of its 618 findings, and the IR's operands in one, so the name is the product's to decide rather than this vocabulary's.
The census found it meaning a statement in all 38 of its findings: go/ast's in the IR and SQL's in a migration runner.
The census found it meaning a pointer in all 12 of its findings, a DNS PTR record's among them, which is a pointer record.

Go's habit for a value of types.Type, since `type` is Go's keyword: the census found it meaning a type in all 82 of its findings. In Go the whole word asks for a descriptive name ending in "Type", as `err` and `ctx` do, since the bare expansion is Go's already. A JSON Web Token's `typ` header is the RFC's own spelling, and the census found it in each consumer's copy of JsonWebToken.ts.
It has three meanings, so every message names them all: the census found it naming a types.Selection in the IR, and once a select statement, while go/ast's `Sel` is a selector.
The census found it naming the IR's anonymous functions and variables in all 5 of its findings.
The census found it once, the IR's function that dereferences a pointer type. "Dereference" is the verb and the noun both.

allowedNames.name: URLSearchParams
allowedNames.reason: A Web API, and not ours to rename.

allowedSegments.reason: MySQL's storage engine, a proper noun. The `Db` in it stands in for nothing, and `InnoDatabase` names a thing that does not exist. Matched as a segment because it appears inside longer names like `InnoDbMaximumIndexKeyBytes`.
